subject: Creativity
title: The 70-20-10 Rule: Google's Innovation Budget
description: A quick win: understand The 70-20-10 Rule: Google's Innovation Budget.

hook.text: Google allocates resources: 70% to core business, 20% to adjacent innovations, 10% to moonshots.

buildup.text: The 70-20-10 model ensures a company innovates at three speeds simultaneously: optimizing today, extending tomorrow.

discovery.text: Most companies spend 95%+ on core business and near-zero on moonshots.

twist.text: Bezos makes the same point: invention requires experiments, and experiments guarantee some failure.

climax.text: The 10% moonshot budget requires accepting that most experiments will fail.

punchline.text: Spend 70% on what works. Spend 10% on what seems crazy.

quiz.question: What does the '10%' in Google's 70-20-10 rule fund?
options: Moonshot projects — risky experiments with transformative potential

details.summary: Google allocates resources using a 70-20-10 rule: 70 percent on core business, 20 percent on related innovations, and 10 percent on experimental moonshots. This structured approach ensures that innovation receives dedicated resources while the core business remains funded and stable.
details.whyItMatters: The 70-20-10 model provides a practical framework for balancing exploitation and exploration. It prevents organizations from either neglecting innovation or abandoning their core business for unproven ideas.
takeaways: Core business gets 70 percent of resources to maintain stability
Adjacent innovations receive 20 percent for growth opportunities
Moonshots get 10 percent for breakthrough potential

faq.question: Did 70-20-10 produce real innovations at Google?
faq.answer: Gmail, Google News, and AdSense all reportedly emerged from the 20 percent allocation. Google X moonshots include self-driving cars and Project Loon. The framework clearly generated significant innovations, though Google has reduced the formalized 20 percent time in recent years.

faq.question: Can small companies use the 70-20-10 model?
faq.answer: Yes, scaled appropriately. Even dedicating one afternoon per week to experimentation or one percent of budget to speculative projects applies the same principle. The key insight is giving innovation dedicated, protected resources rather than hoping it happens spontaneously.
